option: HTML5 + Canvas 2D + vanilla JavaScript (ES modules, zero dependencies) — with PixiJS, Phaser 3 and raw WebGL2 evaluated as nearby alternatives
oneLine: This is the correct stack and the spec already mandates it — the exact genre-defining game in this genre shipped on it (Phaser/HTML5 wrapped in Electron, 1M+ Steam copies before it ever touched Unity) — but 2,000 entities at 60fps is only reachable if spriteAtlas.js pre-renders every shape, emoji and rotation to offscreen canvases at boot instead of drawing paths and fillText per entity per frame.
strengths: GENRE PRECEDENT IS EXACT, NOT ANALOGOUS. Vampire Survivors was an HTML5/Phaser 3 game, free in the browser on itch.io (2021-03-31), then sold on Steam from 2021-12-17 as an Electron wrapper. It hit 1.0 on 2022-10-22 and sold 1M+ copies while still running the Phaser/JS build. The Unity port (version 1.6 onwards per Wikipedia's infobox) came AFTER commercial success, explicitly framed as a mid-2022 milestone to move to an 'industry-standard' engine for performance and to unlock console SKUs. So this stack is proven all the way through 'sold a million copies', and the engine swap was a success-problem, not a launch requirement.

ZERO PORT COST — the spec already IS this stack. Nothing in SECTION 1 needs rewriting. Every hard requirement maps to plain JS: fixed-timestep accumulator (~40 LOC), mulberry32 dual-stream RNG (~20 LOC), object pool (~60 LOC), spatial hash (~80 LOC), localStorage JSON blob + schemaVersion migration (~100 LOC). No engine fights you on any of these; in Phaser or Unity you'd be re-implementing or working around each one.

THE HEADLESS 100x HARNESS IS NEARLY FREE, AND IS THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT FOR THIS STACK. If the sim layer never imports the renderer, the same ES modules run unmodified under `node sim.js` in CI as under `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` in the browser. No headless-engine licence, no CI GPU, no build step, no fake display server. This directly closes the AI agent's feedback loop: change a balance number, run 19 characters x 7 stages headless, read stdout, iterate — with no human touching an editor. Phaser and Pixi both touch document/canvas at import time and make this materially harder; Unity/Godot make it a separate build target.

RENDERER SWAP IS GENUINELY DEFERRABLE. The spec's entities carry a declarative `visual: { shape, color, outline, size, emoji?, sheet?, frames? }` object and gameplay code never touches a canvas context (the `ctx` in AbilityRegistry is a game context, not CanvasRenderingContext2D). That is already the correct seam. Swapping to Pixi later means rewriting renderer.js, spriteAtlas.js, particles.js and damageNumbers.js — roughly 4 files, ~800-1500 LOC — with zero gameplay changes.

CPU-BOUND, NOT RENDER-BOUND, AT 2,000 ENTITIES. At this entity count the frame is dominated by simulation (spatial hash rebuild, 2k broadphase queries, status effects, steering, damage resolution), not by pixels. WebGL's 10-100x sprite headroom is spent on a bottleneck this game does not have. Pixi's own v8 numbers (200k sprites at 60fps) are two orders of magnitude past the requirement.

PUBLISHING IS THE EASIEST OF ANY STACK. Zip the folder, tick 'play in browser' on itch.io, live in 60 seconds — the same distribution path VS itself used to build its audience before Steam. Then Electron + steamworks.js gives Steam achievements, cloud saves and overlay on a well-trodden path.

ITERATION SPEED FOR SOLO DEV + AI AGENT IS THE BEST AVAILABLE. Every file is plain text the agent can read, grep, diff and fully regenerate. No binary scene files, no .meta files, no import pipeline, no compile, no editor state that only exists in a GUI. Edit -> Ctrl+R -> running, sub-second.
dealbreakers: NOT A DEALBREAKER BUT THE #1 PROJECT RISK: the naive implementation of this spec misses the 2,000-entity target by 3-5x. 'Emoji + procedurally drawn shapes' read literally means per-entity `beginPath/arc/fill/stroke` plus `fillText('🧟')` every frame. Color-emoji fillText is among the most expensive Canvas 2D operations that exists (glyph shaping + large color-bitmap raster), and one benchmark found a 16-core 2022 desktop struggling with a couple thousand strings per frame. This must be architected correctly on day one — bake to offscreen canvases at boot — or it becomes a late, painful, whole-render-layer retrofit.

CONSOLE PORTING IS A REWRITE, NOT A WRAPPER. There is no certified third-party JavaScript/Chromium runtime shipping on Switch, PS5 or Xbox for indies. If the game succeeds, the console path is either a Unity/Godot re-implementation (exactly what Poncle did) or a porting house — the same wall VS hit.

SHADER-DRIVEN VFX ARE OFF THE TABLE IN CANVAS 2D. Per-sprite tinting (19 characters needing palette variants), additive glow, bloom, screen distortion on boss phases, hit-flash whites — all of these are one line in Pixi and either impossible or a pre-baked-variants combinatorial mess in Canvas 2D. `ctx.shadowBlur` is the single most expensive 2D property and must never appear per-entity. If the art direction escalates ('loud, screen-filling'), the Pixi swap stops being optional.

PHASER 3 SPECIFICALLY IS A POOR ALTERNATIVE HERE, DESPITE THE VS PRECEDENT. Phaser wants to own the game loop, scene manager, input, physics and pooling — all four of which the spec defines itself with stricter requirements (fixed 60Hz accumulator, custom spatial hash, zero-alloc pools). You would fight it, ship 1MB of unused framework, and make the headless harness harder. Take the VS precedent as 'JS + Canvas/WebGL works commercially', not 'use Phaser'.

RAW WEBGL2 IS THE WRONG PLACE TO SPEND A SOLO DEV'S BUDGET. You'd own a sprite batcher, atlas packer, shader pipeline, blend-state manager and a text renderer — call it 2,000-4,000 LOC of infrastructure before the first enemy appears — to solve a bottleneck the game doesn't have at 2k entities. Use Pixi if you ever need WebGL.

'MID-RANGE LAPTOP' IS UNDEFINED IN THE SPEC AND THAT AMBIGUITY IS DANGEROUS. Intel UHD 620 at 1080p and Iris Xe / Ryzen 5 4500U are very different targets (the older benchmark data shows ~2x swing from GPU alone). Pin a reference machine and a reference resolution before claiming the target is met.

iOS SAFARI CAN EVICT localStorage AFTER ~7 DAYS OF NON-USE (ITP). For a gacha game where the entire meta-layer is the retention hook, silent save loss is severe. Mitigate with IndexedDB plus a copy-pasteable export/import save code.

facts.claim: Vampire Survivors' Wikipedia infobox lists its engine verbatim as 'Phaser (pre-version 1.6)' and 'Unity (version 1.6 onwards)'.

The Unity migration was motivated by a stated milestone slated for mid-2022 to port the game to an 'industry-standard' game engine to improve its overall performance — i.e. it happened after commercial success, not before launch.
Vampire Survivors was originally coded in HTML5 with Phaser 3 and released free as a browser game on itch.io on 2021-03-31, nine months before Steam.
Steam Early Access launched 2021-12-17 at $2.99; full 1.0 release for Windows/macOS on 2022-10-20.
The Steam PC build of Vampire Survivors was an Electron wrapper around the HTML5/Phaser game — identifiable by its large executable and Chromium .pak files.
facts.source: https://github.com/TechnoLustMatty/Electron-Game-Hacking-Vampire-Survivors- ('Vampire Survivors was made using Electron and you can usually tell based on the massive executable file and the .pak files')

facts.claim: The Phaser-based Vampire Survivors sold over one million copies on Steam before the Unity port.

The exact calendar date of the Unity port (version 1.6) could not be pinned within research budget, so the precise ordering of the Unity port versus the Xbox (2022-11-10) and mobile (2022-12-08) SKUs is unconfirmed.
Console/platform rollout: Xbox One & Series X/S 2022-11-10; Android & iOS 2022-12-08; Nintendo Switch 2023-08-17; PS4 & PS5 2024-08-29; Meta Quest 2025-11-13.

On a genuinely mid-range laptop (AMD Ryzen 5 4500U, 8GB, Windows 11, Edge 109), rendering 10,000 sprites: Kontra 60 FPS, Babylon.js 56, Pixi.js 47, Phaser 43, Kaboom/Kaplay 3. Kontra used fixed-timestep animation, which the author flags as flattering its number.

Kontra — the library that hit 60 FPS at 10,000 sprites in that benchmark — is a Canvas 2D micro-engine, not WebGL. If true this is a direct Canvas-2D-at-10k-sprites data point, ~5x the spec's requirement.
facts.source: Could not verify within budget — Kontra docs URL returned 404. Treat the 10k figure as unconfirmed for Canvas 2D specifically.

facts.claim: Older Canvas 2D sprite benchmark (2013, Sony Vaio): Intel HD3000 managed 1,100 sprites at 60 FPS and 2,900 at 30 FPS; the same laptop's nVidia GT330m managed 2,500 at 60 FPS and 5,400 at 30 FPS — roughly 2x purely from GPU. Note this is 2011-era hardware; a 2020+ integrated GPU is far faster.
drawImage is materially faster when x/y are rounded to whole numbers; sub-pixel coordinates force the browser to interpolate, costing time and blurring the sprite.

canvas fillText is a severe bottleneck: a 16-core desktop system in 2022 struggled to display a couple of thousand strings at 60 FPS; font parsing overhead can make text rendering up to ~3x slower, with parsing taking ~2x longer than the actual raster.

PixiJS v8 renders 200,000 sprites in a Container at 60fps and 1,000,000 particles in a ParticleContainer at 60fps; v7->v8, 100k moving sprites went from ~50ms to ~15ms CPU time per frame, and 100k static sprites from ~21ms to ~0.12ms.

Electron and NW.js are the only desktop frameworks officially supported by the two main Steam distribution libraries (steamworks.js and greenworks). Tauri has documented problems getting the Steam overlay to work.

Electron produces builds over 100MB (Chromium + Node bundled) but offers maximum compatibility; Tauri/Neutralino/Wails produce far smaller builds but use OS-native webviews (WebKit on macOS/Linux) that sacrifice graphics performance and struggle with WebGL-heavy workloads.

steamworks.js is the actively maintained Steamworks binding (~300 weekly npm downloads); greenworks was originally built by Greenheart Games to ship Game Dev Tycoon on Steam, is stable and used in production, but the original repo has been inactive ~8 years and only a community fork is maintained.
Athena Crisis shipped to macOS on Steam via Electron — a second named commercial precedent for the web-game-to-Steam path.
itch.io hosts HTML5 games played directly in the browser (upload a zip with index.html at root, set viewport, tick 'play in browser'), and the revenue share is developer-chosen and can be set to 0%.

Poki serves 60M+ monthly active users and curates tightly (quality thresholds for gameplay, art and technical performance); CrazyGames reaches ~35M monthly users, accepts a wider range of genres, and offers +50% revenue share for agreeing to 2 months' launch exclusivity. Both require SDK integration; review takes days (small portals) to weeks (Poki).

Capacitor uses WKWebView on iOS (full JIT access, so JS runs at native browser speed) and the system WebView on Android (performance varies by OS version and device), and explicitly supports canvas and WebGL games. A known iOS failure mode is the 'white screen of death' when iOS kills web content for excessive memory use.

There is no practical certified JavaScript/Chromium runtime for third-party indies on Switch, PS5 or Xbox; running a game in a browser on consoles is described by practitioners as hard and non-optimal, with the recommended path being a port to C++/a real engine, usually via a publisher or specialist porting house.
Steam Direct charges a $100 recoupable fee per app submitted.

entityPerfNotes:
YES — 2,000+ entities at 60fps on a mid-range laptop is achievable in Canvas 2D, but ONLY under a specific discipline. Frame budget at 60fps is 16.67ms; the sim (spatial hash + 2k broadphase + damage + status) should target under 6ms, leaving ~8ms for render with 2ms of slack.

WHAT ACTUALLY DOMINATES THE FRAME:
Canvas 2D in Chrome/Edge/Firefox is GPU-accelerated (Skia over D3D/Metal), so this is NOT fill-rate bound at 2k small sprites. The cost is per-call JS-to-native overhead plus driver state flushes. Ranked worst to best for this game:
1. `fillText` with color emoji — catastrophic. Glyph shaping plus a large color-bitmap raster, per call. 2,000 of these per frame will not hit 60fps on any laptop. A 16-core desktop reportedly struggles with a couple thousand strings/frame.
2. `ctx.font` assignment — font string re-parsing costs up to 2x the actual raster. Never set it inside a loop.
3. `ctx.shadowBlur` / shadow* — the single most expensive 2D property. Must be zero, always. Bake outlines and glows into the sprite.
4. Per-entity path construction (`beginPath` + `arc`/`quadraticCurveTo` + `fill` + `stroke`) — the spec's literal 'procedurally drawn shapes'. Roughly 5-15x the cost of an equivalent `drawImage`, and it is the difference between hitting and missing the target.
5. `save()`/`restore()` and `setTransform` for rotation — cheap-ish individually, brutal at 2k/frame.
6. `fillStyle`/`globalAlpha`/`globalCompositeOperation` changes — each can force a batch flush.
7. `drawImage` at integer coordinates from a pre-rendered source — the cheap path. This is the only thing that should be in the hot loop.

WHERE IT FALLS OVER:
- Naive (per-entity paths + emoji fillText + shadowBlur + save/restore): expect the wall at roughly 300-800 entities on a mid-range laptop. Confidence: likely, not measured.
- Disciplined (everything blitted from pre-rendered offscreen canvases, integer coords, no shadows, state sorted): 5,000-15,000 drawImage calls/frame is realistic on 2020+ integrated graphics. 2,000 sits comfortably inside with headroom for particles (capped 800) and damage numbers (capped 60). Anchors: 2011-era Intel HD3000 did 1,100 Canvas 2D sprites at 60fps; a Ryzen 5 4500U laptop ran 10,000 sprites at 47fps through Pixi in a 2023 benchmark, so the same machine's raw throughput is an order of magnitude past what 2,000 needs.

THE TECHNIQUES THAT GET YOU THERE — spriteAtlas.js must do ALL of this at boot, not later:
- PROCEDURAL PRE-RENDER. Every distinct `visual` variant (shape x color x size x outline) is drawn ONCE into a small offscreen canvas at init. Hot loop only ever calls drawImage. This is the single highest-leverage change and it costs nothing to do from day one — reframe spriteAtlas.js from 'future real-art module' to 'the renderer's only source of pixels', which conveniently makes the real-art drop-in path a no-op later.
- BAKE EMOJI. Render each emoji once into an offscreen canvas at boot; blit thereafter. Zero fillText for entities, ever.
- BITMAP DIGIT ATLAS for damage numbers. Pre-render glyphs 0-9, '+', '!', 'x', crit variants at 2-3 sizes; compose numbers from blits. This removes text from the hot path entirely and makes the 60-number cap trivially cheap.
- PRE-BAKED ROTATION FRAMES. 16 or 32 angle steps per rotating sprite instead of save/rotate/restore per entity.
- SORT DRAWS BY STATE. One pass per (atlas page, globalAlpha bucket, composite mode). Additive particles drawn as one contiguous block with a single `globalCompositeOperation` set/reset, not toggled per particle.
- NO save()/restore() IN THE LOOP. Set camera transform once per layer with `setTransform`, draw in world coords, reset once.
- ROUND COORDINATES. `(x + 0.5) | 0` before drawImage — faster and sharper.
- CULL HARD. On a 4000x4000 stage with a ~1920x1080 viewport, the drawn set is a fraction of the 2,000 alive. The spec's off-screen culling plus cheap-update rules already handle this; make the cull test AABB-against-camera before the draw call, not inside it.
- DIRTY RECTS: SKIP THEM. A scrolling-camera bullet-heaven redraws essentially the whole screen every frame. Dirty-rect bookkeeping is pure overhead here. Full clear (or one background blit) is correct.
- Consider `ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { alpha: false })` — lets the compositor skip per-frame blending of the canvas layer.

HEADROOM FROM SWAPPING TO WEBGL/PIXI:
Large but largely wasted at this scale — roughly 10-50x on sprite throughput (Pixi v8: 200k sprites at 60fps, 1M particles via ParticleContainer). At 2,000 entities you become CPU/simulation-bound before render-bound, so the swap does not raise your entity ceiling much; what it actually buys is CAPABILITY: free per-sprite tint (19 character palettes without pre-baking every variant), additive glow and blend modes without state-flush cost, full-screen shader filters for boss phases and hit-stop, and cheap rotation/scale. Buy Pixi when the art direction demands it, not when the entity count does.

CAN THE SWAP BE DEFERRED? Yes, and the spec is already shaped for it — gameplay code never touches a canvas context and entities carry only a declarative `visual` object. Two things to get right NOW so the door stays open: (1) keep renderer.js a narrow IMMEDIATE-MODE API — `beginFrame/setCamera/drawSprite(atlasId, x, y, rot, scale, alpha, tint)/drawText/endFrame` — and let any future Pixi backend maintain the retained-mode scene graph internally; (2) note that Pixi is retained-mode, so the entity pool would also need to pool Sprite display objects. That's a real refactor of the pool layer, not a one-line change — but it is ~4 render files plus the pool, and zero gameplay files.
publishingPaths:
itch.io — EASIEST OF ANY STACK, AND THE PROVEN ON-RAMP FOR THIS EXACT GENRE. Zip the folder with index.html at root, upload, tick 'this file will be played in the browser', set viewport dimensions, publish. Free to host, and YOU choose the revenue share (can be 0%). This is literally where Vampire Survivors built its audience for nine months before Steam. For a zero-dependency, no-build-step game the upload artifact IS the source tree. Ship an early build here for free playtesting and wishlist-driving.

Newgrounds — accepts HTML5 zips, has its own medals/scoreboards API and ad revenue share. Worth doing purely for audience fit: the anime/VTuber aesthetic lands well there and discovery for new games is better than most portals.

CrazyGames (~35M MAU) / Poki (60M+ MAU) — both require SDK integration (preroll/rewarded ads), pass a quality and technical review, and take days-to-weeks. Poki is tightly curated and hard to get into; CrazyGames is broader and offers +50% revenue share for 2 months' launch exclusivity. IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR THIS GAME: portal economics assume short sessions and stateless play. A 20-minute-run roguelite whose entire hook is persistent gacha meta-progression stored in localStorage is a poor structural fit — portal iframes and third-party-storage rules make saves fragile, and a player who loses their roster churns permanently. Treat portals as top-of-funnel marketing that drives Steam wishlists, not as the revenue line.

STEAM — THE ACTUAL BUSINESS, AND A WELL-TRODDEN PATH.
Wrapper: ELECTRON. Not a close call. Electron and NW.js are the only desktop frameworks officially supported by the Steamworks binding libraries, the Steam overlay works with both, and Chromium's own compositor gives you predictable graphics performance across machines. NW.js is a viable equal-second (Game Dev Tycoon shipped on it, and greenworks was originally built by Greenheart Games for exactly that). TAURI IS THE WRONG CHOICE HERE despite its appeal: it uses OS-native webviews (WebKitGTK on Linux, WKWebView on macOS) which sacrifice graphics performance, it has documented Steam-overlay breakage, and neither Steam binding officially supports it. The 100MB+ Electron bundle vs Tauri's ~5-10MB is a non-issue on Steam — nobody has ever refunded an indie roguelite over download size.
Steamworks binding: steamworks.js (actively maintained, npm-installable) preferred over greenworks (stable and production-proven but the original repo has been dormant ~8 years; only a community fork lives).
Achievements: straightforward via steamworks.js — fire on the same events your in-game achievement system already fires.
CLOUD SAVES — ONE GOTCHA WORTH CALLING OUT: Steam Auto-Cloud syncs FILES. Your localStorage lives inside Chromium's Local Storage LevelDB inside the Electron user-data dir, which is not a clean thing to sync. Under Electron, write the save JSON to a real file via Node `fs` (into `app.getPath('userData')`) and point Auto-Cloud at it. Keep the browser build on localStorage. That means save.js needs a tiny pluggable storage backend from the start — a ~30 LOC abstraction, trivial now, annoying to retrofit.
Named precedents for web-game-to-Steam: Vampire Survivors (Electron, 1M+ copies), Game Dev Tycoon (NW.js), Athena Crisis (Electron, macOS Steam). Cost: $100 recoupable Steam Direct fee per app (likely, not verified this session).

MOBILE — see below; both browser and Capacitor-wrapped native paths are open, which is more than most engines give you for free.
portCostFromSpec:
ZERO. The spec mandates this exact stack in SECTION 1, and every hard requirement it lists is a natural fit for plain JS rather than a workaround. Nothing gets rewritten. What I would ADD to the spec (small, cheap now, expensive later):

1. REDEFINE spriteAtlas.js AS MANDATORY-AT-BOOT, NOT FUTURE-ART-ONLY. Today the spec frames it as 'a documented drop-in path so real art can replace placeholders later'. It should instead be the renderer's ONLY source of pixels from day one: at boot it rasterizes every `visual` variant (shapes, outlines, colors, sizes), every emoji, and every needed rotation step into offscreen canvases. The hot loop then only calls drawImage. This is what makes 2,000 entities land, AND it makes the real-art swap a genuine no-op later. ~150 LOC. Add a hard rule alongside the existing performance rules: 'No beginPath, no fillText, no shadowBlur, no save/restore inside the per-entity draw loop.'

2. ADD A BITMAP DIGIT ATLAS to damageNumbers.js. Removes fillText from the hot path entirely.

3. MAKE renderer.js EXPLICITLY IMMEDIATE-MODE with a narrow API (beginFrame/setCamera/drawSprite/drawText/endFrame). Costs nothing now, and is the precondition for a later Pixi backend.

4. ADD A PLUGGABLE STORAGE BACKEND to save.js (localStorage in browser, Node fs under Electron, IndexedDB on iOS). ~30 LOC now; required for Steam Cloud and for surviving iOS ITP eviction.

5. PIN THE PERF TARGET. 'Mid-range laptop' needs a named reference machine and resolution, plus an automated perf gate — spawn 2,500 entities via a `?perf=1` flag and assert p95 frame time under 16.6ms in the F3 overlay.

PORT COST TO THE ALTERNATIVES, if you chose one instead:
- PixiJS: rewrite renderer.js, spriteAtlas.js, particles.js, damageNumbers.js plus retained-mode Sprite pooling in pool.js. ~10-15% of the codebase, 0% of gameplay/data. Also softly breaks 'zero dependencies / no build step' — you can vendor Pixi as an ES module and keep no-build, but it's a ~400KB dependency and a real one. Defensible later, unnecessary now.
- Phaser 3: rewrite ~30-40% of the spec's core architecture. Phaser wants to own the loop, scene manager, input and physics, all of which the spec specifies itself with stricter contracts (fixed 60Hz accumulator, custom spatial hash, zero-alloc pooling). It also complicates the headless 100x harness, which is a first-class requirement here. The VS precedent argues for HTML5 as a shipping stack — it does not argue for Phaser as the right architecture for a spec this opinionated.
- Raw WebGL2: same 4 render files PLUS ~2,000-4,000 LOC of engine infrastructure you own forever (batcher, atlas packer, shaders, blend state, text). Wrong investment for a solo dev whose real bottleneck is content volume — 19 characters x 4 ability pillars, 7 stages, gacha, relics, evolutions.
